items.prompt: assertRefundAllowed's third parameter is named capturedAmountMinor. What value does the refund service actually pass in that slot?
items.answer: The remaining refundable amount, amountMinor minus the SUCCEEDED refunds
distractors: The original captured amount, Payment.amountMinor, unchanged by earlier refunds
The sum of every refund row on the payment, with PENDING rows included
The amount the operator typed into the refund form, re-validated by Zod
items.explanation: Line 33 computes remainingRefundableAmount = payment.amountMinor - refundedAmount and passes it on line 34; the guide calls the parameter name misleading for exactly this reason.

items.prompt: A FAILED payment of 100 receives a refund request for 500. Which error code comes back?
items.answer: PAYMENT_NOT_REFUNDABLE, because the status check runs before the amount check
distractors: REFUND_AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_CAPTURE, because 500 is the larger of the two violations
INVALID_PAYMENT_TRANSITION, because the refund is checked as a transition first
Both codes together, collected into error.details as a list of violations
items.explanation: assertRefundAllowed throws on the first failing check; status (lines 55-57) is tested before amount (lines 60-62), so the amount is never examined.

items.prompt: During one successful createRefundForPayment call, which statuses does the new Refund row hold, and when?
items.answer: PENDING when created, then SUCCEEDED later in the same transaction
distractors: SUCCEEDED from the start, as the simulated provider never fails
PENDING until a provider webhook arrives and marks it SUCCEEDED
PENDING, then REFUNDED once the payment total has been covered
items.explanation: createRefund writes status: RefundStatus.PENDING; after the REFUND_REQUESTED event the service calls transitionRefundStatus(refund.id, RefundStatus.SUCCEEDED, providerRefundId, tx), all inside the one prisma.$transaction.

items.prompt: You add SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the payment row at the start of the transaction. Two concurrent 40-unit refunds hit a 100 payment with 60 refunded. What does the second request receive?
items.answer: 409 PAYMENT_NOT_REFUNDABLE: after waiting it sees the first refund flipped it to REFUNDED
distractors: 409 REFUND_AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_CAPTURE: after waiting it sees a refunded total of 100 against 100
200: the lock only orders the two requests and never changes what the check sees
A deadlock error: both transactions try to lock the same payment row at once
items.explanation: The first request fully refunds the payment and sets status REFUNDED; B's read waits, then sees REFUNDED, and status is checked before amount.

items.prompt: Same row lock in place, but now two concurrent 20-unit refunds arrive against a 100 payment with 70 already refunded. Why does the second one fail with REFUND_AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_CAPTURE rather than PAYMENT_NOT_REFUNDABLE?
items.answer: A's refund was partial, so the payment stays SUCCEEDED and B fails on amount (20 > 10)
distractors: The lock is released before the status check runs, so B does not see A's committed write
Partial refunds set status PARTIALLY_REFUNDED, and that status skips the status check
Two requests queued on a lock run the amount check before the status check
items.explanation: Only a full refund flips the payment to REFUNDED (refundService.ts:64-75); after A the total is 90 with status SUCCEEDED, so B reaches the amount check.

items.prompt: In a real integration where the provider confirms refunds asynchronously, why would the current aggregate let two operators each refund the full balance?
items.answer: The sum counts only SUCCEEDED refunds, so a PENDING refund reserves no money
distractors: The refunded sum is cached per operator session, so it goes stale
PENDING refunds are deleted when the provider is slow, which frees the balance
The aggregate runs outside the transaction, so it cannot see newly inserted rows
items.explanation: sumSuccessfulRefundsForPayment filters status: SUCCEEDED; today the window is tiny only because the refund is flipped to SUCCEEDED in the same transaction.

items.prompt: An operator double-clicks the refund form's submit button and the balance allows both. What happens, and what would prevent it?
items.answer: Two refunds; only an idempotency key on the refund endpoint would stop it
distractors: One refund; the transaction rejects any repeat as a duplicate write
One refund, because the refund endpoint reuses the payment's idempotency record
Both fail, because the second request sees the first's PENDING refund and aborts
items.explanation: A transaction makes one request atomic; idempotency makes a repeated request harmless. Only payment creation has an idempotency key.

items.prompt: User B sends POST /api/payments with the same Idempotency-Key and identical body that user A used earlier. What does B get?
items.answer: A replay of A's response, including A's payment id, since the key is not user-scoped
distractors: 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED_WITH_DIFFERENT_PAYLOAD, because the user differs
A brand-new payment of its own, since each user has a separate key namespace
400 MISSING_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY, because user A's request already consumed the key
items.explanation: findIdempotencyRecord(route, key) ignores the user, and the fingerprint covers only the body, so identical bodies match and B receives A's completed response.

items.prompt: The payment endpoint requires an Idempotency-Key, yet a double-submitted create-payment form still creates two payments. Why?
items.answer: The create hook generates a fresh Idempotency-Key on every single mutation call
distractors: The server always ignores the key when the request body is byte-for-byte identical
The key is only stored after the payment commits, so both requests miss the lookup
The browser strips custom headers like Idempotency-Key from retried POSTs
items.explanation: usePaymentActions sends crypto.randomUUID() as the Idempotency-Key per mutation, so each submission looks new. A retry must carry the same key for idempotency to work.

items.prompt: An OPS user refunds 30 of a SUCCEEDED 100 payment that has nothing refunded yet. What HTTP status and paymentStatus does the response carry?
items.answer: 202, with paymentStatus SUCCEEDED since the refund is partial
distractors: 201, with paymentStatus SUCCEEDED, as a new Refund row was made
200, with paymentStatus PARTIALLY_REFUNDED for the partial amount
202, with paymentStatus REFUNDED, as any refund flips the payment
items.explanation: The route returns jsonOk(result, 202). fullyRefunded is 0 + 30 === 100, which is false, so the payment is not transitioned and the result reports payment.status, still SUCCEEDED.

items.prompt: After fully refunding a SUCCEED-mode payment, reconciliation records an issue for it on every run. Which issue, and what did the refund path forget?
items.answer: STATUS_MISMATCH: the refund path never updates ProviderPayment.status
distractors: AMOUNT_MISMATCH: the refunded total is not written back to Payment.amountMinor
MISSING_WEBHOOK: refunds create no webhook delivery row for the payment
None: reconciliation skips REFUNDED payments, so no issue is recorded
items.explanation: Reconciliation maps the provider's SUCCEEDED to SUCCEEDED and compares it with the local REFUNDED, flagging a mismatch each time.

items.prompt: The webhook service marks a bad event REJECTED using tx and then rethrows. What evidence of the failed webhook survives in WebhookEvent?
items.answer: Nothing survives: the rethrow rolls back the event row and its REJECTED mark
distractors: The REJECTED row: status updates commit independently of the rethrown error
The RECEIVED row: the insert commits before the REJECTED update is attempted
Both rows: Prisma commits each statement before the callback finishes
items.explanation: Writes made with tx share the transaction's fate; only the outbound WebhookDelivery records the failure.

items.front: Three standard fixes for concurrent over-refunds under READ COMMITTED
items.back: 1) Lock the payment row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) so B waits for A. 2) Run at Serializable isolation and retry on serialization failure. 3) Keep a running refundedMinor on Payment and update it with a guarded atomic UPDATE ... WHERE refunded + n <= amount, treating zero rows as 409.

items.front: Why moving reads into the transaction does not solve real provider coordination
items.back: The provider refund id is generated locally (prov_ref_<uuid>) with no external call. A real provider refund can succeed after the DB transaction rolls back, or vice versa; that needs an outbox or a request-then-confirm-via-webhook design.

items.front: How jsonError maps errors, and why the refund service catches nothing
items.back: RouteError -> { error: { code, message, details } } with its status; ZodError -> 400; anything else -> logged 500. The service lets non-domain errors propagate so infrastructure failures stay distinguishable from domain refusals.

items.front: What happens when one provider event is delivered twice concurrently?
items.back: The duplicate check reads the event before the transaction, so both deliveries proceed; the second createWebhookEvent hits the providerEventId unique constraint and surfaces as a 500.
